The Library of Unfinished Things

There is a library I go to in my head when I can't sleep.

It's not a quiet library. It's not the one with the rolling ladders and the stained glass where everyone whispers and the dust motes hang in the sun. This one is loud in its own way.

Every shelf holds something unfinished.

On the first floor, there are the half-written letters. Thousands of them. Some are folded neatly, some are crumpled. "Dear Mom, I never told you that..." "Hey man, about last summer..." "To whoever finds this..." I walk past them and I can feel the weight of not sending them.

On the second floor are the projects. Half-knitted sweaters with one sleeve too long. Canvases with only the sky painted in. Novels that stop on page 43, mid-sentence. A birdhouse with no roof. A language learned halfway — someone can order coffee and ask for directions, but not say "I miss you." All the things we started when we were briefly, brightly sure of who we were going to become.

The top floor is the heaviest. That's where the versions of ourselves are. The kid who almost made varsity but quit. The girl who almost moved to Berlin. The man who almost said yes. They stand there like mannequins, not sad, not angry, just... waiting. Looking out the windows at a life that never quite arrived.

I found myself in this library again last Tuesday. In real life, it was 2:17 a.m. My phone was face-down on the nightstand. The fridge was humming. My apartment was too warm.

You know that feeling when you are tired but your brain refuses to get the memo? It just keeps pacing.

I got up and made tea I didn't want and sat at my kitchen table. And I thought about how strange it is that we all live with ghosts, but not the spooky kind. Just the ghosts of our own intentions.

Someone once told me that the average person has had about seven distinct dreams for their life by the time they're 30. Not sleeping dreams — waking ones. Astronaut, baker, parent, runaway, professor, musician, quiet-person-with-a-dog-in-the-woods. We collect them like ticket stubs. Proof we went somewhere, even if we didn't stay.

I used to want to be a cartographer. Not kidding. When I was nine, my grandfather gave me an old atlas. The pages were soft at the edges. Countries that didn't exist anymore were still printed there, in faded pastel colors. The USSR spread across two pages like a sleeping giant. I loved that a book could be out of date and still be true, in a way.

I would draw maps of imaginary places. The Sea of Lost Socks. The Mountains of Maybe. I had careful legends and scales. "Here be monsters, but friendly ones."

At some point I stopped. No big moment. I just... started drawing other things. College applications. Five-year plans. My maps got smaller and more practical, until I wasn't drawing them at all.

I think that's what happens. You don't lose the old dreams all at once. You just file them away. You tell yourself you'll come back later. Later is the most patient lie we tell.

At the kitchen table, with my stupid tea getting cold, I did something I hadn't done in twenty years. I found a piece of printer paper and a cheap ballpoint pen and I started to draw a map.

It was terrible. My islands were lopsided. My compass rose looked like a starfish having a bad day. But I kept going. I drew the Library of Unfinished Things right in the middle, because of course it belongs on every map. I drew the ocean around it and labeled it "The Ongoing."

I realized I was smiling. Not a big cinematic smile. Just a small, private one. The kind you do when no one is watching.

Here's what I've been thinking about since then: maybe unfinished isn't the same as failed.

We treat our lives like we are supposed to be building a single, perfect structure. A tower, straight up. Every brick in place. But what if it's not a tower? What if it's a city? Sprawling, messy, contradictory. Some beautiful buildings, some abandoned lots. Some roads that go nowhere. That's not failure. That's just what a city looks like when people actually live in it.

The half-knitted sweater still kept someone warm for a little while, while it was being made. The letter you never sent still helped you figure out what you needed to say. The kid who almost made varsity still learned how to run until his lungs burned.

Nothing is wasted. Even the detours leave pavement.

I think we like to imagine there are two kinds of people: the ones who finish everything they start, and the ones who don't. The winners and the quitters. But I don't know anyone like that. The most disciplined person I know still has a junk drawer. The most scattered person I know still waters her plants every single day without fail.

We all finish some things and abandon others. Our job isn't to finish everything. It's to notice which unfinished things still tug at our sleeve.

Not everything on those shelves needs to be completed. Some of it belongs there. That angry letter you wrote at 1 a.m. six years ago? Good thing you didn't send it. That MLM your cousin tried to recruit you into? Good thing you quit.

But some things are still asking for you.

So here's my new, very unscientific theory: once a month, go to your library. Walk the floors. Pick up one thing. Just one. Dust it off. Ask it, "Do you still want to be made?"

If the answer is no, let it stay there with kindness. It served its purpose. If the answer is yes — even a quiet, embarrassed yes — take it downstairs with you. Carry it back into the world.

Mine was maps. Yours might be sourdough. Or Spanish. Or that apology. Or running a 5K. Or finally planting those seeds that have been in the drawer since spring.

It doesn't have to be big. It just has to be honest.

I taped my terrible map to the fridge. It's crooked. My roommate will probably think a five-year-old made it. I don't care. Every time I go to get milk, I see it. The Sea of Lost Socks is still there, waiting.

And the Library, I think, is a little less crowded than it was before.

There is still a lot I haven't done. There is still a lot I probably never will do. But the paper is still on the table. The pen still works.

That, for now, is enough.
